antigen.def: Any molecule that a lymphocyte's antigen receptor or an antibody binds specifically. Each antigen receptor binds one small part of it, an epitope (antigenic determinant), and a large antigen carries many epitopes.

t-cell.def: A lymphocyte that matures in the thymus (as a thymocyte, passing positive and negative selection) and recognizes, with its T cell receptor, only short peptides held on MHC proteins. Some kill infected cells; others coordinate responses.

b-cell.def: A lymphocyte that matures in the red bone marrow and binds intact antigen with a membrane-bound antibody as its antigen receptor; when activated, its descendants release antibodies.

mhc.def: Membrane glycoproteins coded by the major histocompatibility complex that hold peptides for T cells to inspect. Class I, on nearly all nucleated cells, shows peptides made inside the cell; class II, mainly on antigen-presenting cells, shows peptides from material taken in. Their genes vary enormously between people (MHC polymorphism).

apc.def: A cell that takes in antigen, breaks it into peptides and loads them onto MHC class II (antigen processing), then displays them for T cells (antigen presentation): dendritic cells, which start naive T cell responses, macrophages and B cells.

self-tolerance.def: The state in which lymphocytes do not attack your own tissues. Central tolerance removes self-reactive lymphocytes as they mature (negative selection and clonal deletion in the thymus, a similar test in the marrow); peripheral tolerance silences those that escape, for example by clonal anergy when a T cell binds self antigen without a second, confirming signal.

clonal-selection.def: Activation of only the rare naive lymphocytes whose ready-made antigen receptors fit an antigen, followed by clonal expansion into a clone of identical cells; many clones responding to one microbe's many epitopes make a polyclonal response.

immune-memory.def: The ability to respond faster and more strongly to an antigen met before, carried by long-lived memory B cells and memory T cells left after clonal expansion, which are more numerous and quicker to switch on than the naive cells they came from.
